# U01 — Programming you can explain

**Foundations · Learning unassessed.** Write, run, test and explain a small program from a blank function.

Prerequisites: None. Start with FIRST_SESSION.md.. Challenge-out requires evidence; see ASSESSMENT.md.

## Learn

A program transforms inputs into outputs. A variable names a value; a function names a reusable transformation. Parameters receive inputs and return sends a result to the caller. Logging displays a value but does not return it. A condition chooses a path; a loop repeats an action. An array is an ordered collection; an object groups named properties. Trace a concrete example on paper before adding syntax. Files, the terminal working directory and error messages are part of programming. Read FIRST_SESSION.md for a complete first lesson with setup, vocabulary and a 75-minute sequence.

- Values include numbers, strings, booleans and undefined. === compares without coercion.
- const prevents rebinding; it does not freeze an array. Avoid changing caller-owned input accidentally.
- A test assertion compares actual behavior to a stated expectation; read its first relevant file and line.
- Git status lists changes; diff shows edits. Commit only changes you can explain.

## Worked example

```text
function countWarm(readings) {
  let count = 0;
  for (const reading of readings) {
    if (reading >= 20) count = count + 1;
  }
  return count;
}
console.log(countWarm([19, 20, 24])); // 2
```

For 19, count stays 0. For 20 it becomes 1, and 24 makes it 2. The boundary is inclusive because of >=. Empty input never enters the loop, so returns 0. The independent exercise uses a different rule.

## Guided practice

1. Follow FIRST_SESSION.md; confirm node --version in the repository terminal.
2. Type the temperature example into a scratch file; predict results for [] and [20] before running it.
3. Change the threshold into a second parameter and explain which lines depend on it.
4. Run the unfinished U01 checks and read one failure. Seek a concept hint if needed; type the code yourself.

## U01-01 — Trace and change a small function

**PAIR · Learn with guidance · 2–4 focused hours, provisional.**

Work through the temperature example. Use a tutor for explanation and one hint at a time.

Acceptance:

- Trace [19,20,24], [] and [20] on paper.
- Make threshold an argument and demonstrate two values.
- Explain your working directory, git diff and one test failure.

Done:

- Acceptance checked against actual output and a learner-owned artifact.
- Help used recorded; learner explains behavior and limitations.
- Feedback and delayed transfer pending until performed. Agent-prepared code earns no learning credit.

Out of scope: Extra frameworks, real notifications, paid infrastructure and unrelated platform work. Use synthetic data and the smallest exercise that proves the skill.

## U01-02 — Implement the task summary

**SOLO · Build independently · 2–4 focused hours, provisional.**

In practice/learner/u01.mjs implement remainingTitles(tasks): return titles whose done is exactly false, in original order. Input is an array of {title:string,done:boolean}. Also implement totalMinutes(values): sum nonnegative integer minutes. Inputs are valid; neither function may mutate them.

## U01-03 — Transfer to a study budget

**SOLO · Transfer independently · 2–4 focused hours, provisional.**

In a new file implement fitSessions(durations,budget). Return a consecutive prefix whose sum stays <= budget. Stop at the first duration that cannot fit; do not skip it. All inputs are nonnegative integers. Preserve input.

Acceptance:

- [20,30,10] with budget 45 returns [20]; with 50 returns [20,30].
- Test empty input, zero budget and a zero-minute session.
- Write your own assertion and explain why filtering durations individually is wrong.

Done:

- Acceptance checked against actual output and a learner-owned artifact.

## Delayed transfer

Return the first title longer than a supplied length, or null. Define equality behavior and test that boundary.

Revisit after 2–7 days and around three weeks with the prior solution closed. These are scheduling defaults, not scientific mastery thresholds.

## Debugging scenario

Predict what happens when a function logs 7 and its caller adds the return value to 1. Explain undefined from the observation.

Injected defects belong only in disposable copies with synthetic data and external effects disabled.

## If stuck

Trace three values on paper. Write a one-input function before returning to the loop. If the terminal is the obstacle, repeat only FIRST_SESSION setup.

## Readiness

Demonstrate both competencies on your own task and a changed example. Apply ASSESSMENT.md; ratings describe behavior, not job titles.

Keep small-exercise records to three lines: intention; result/artifact; help/next gap. Portfolio work also needs a plan, review and handoff.
